content.text:
Yes. We should build a shared hook layer now and defer MCP-dependent hooks until Wisp and Monokl are stable.

We already have the beginnings in [`shared/hooks/`](/Users/gabe/Projects/agent-plugins/shared/hooks): `pre-command.sh` and `subagent-start.sh`. They are reference scripts today; they are not yet wired into either harness’s plugin lifecycle configuration.

Claude supports this particularly well: plugin-level `hooks/hooks.json`, plus hooks scoped directly to a skill or agent. It can inject subagent context, run post-edit checks, and block unsafe tool operations. [Claude hook reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks)

Codex supports the same broad pattern through plugin lifecycle hooks, including `SessionStart`, `SubagentStart`, `PreToolUse`, and `PostToolUse`; its `SubagentStart` hook can inject concise developer context into the spawned agent. [Codex hooks](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/hooks)

We should share policy, not hook implementations:

| Policy | Shared source | Claude adapter | Codex adapter |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| JIT language/tool context | `shared/hooks/` policy + detector | `SubagentStart` | `SubagentStart` |
| Protected-path / unsafe-command checks | Shared rule data | `PreToolUse` | `PreToolUse` |
| Deterministic post-edit validation | Shared validator scripts | `PostToolUse` | `PostToolUse` |
| Artifact persistence reminders | Shared schema/path rules | Session or tool hook | Session or tool hook |

The adapters must remain native. Claude and Codex have different event payloads, environment variables, decision formats, and lifecycle behavior. For example, Claude can use `SubagentStop` to keep a subagent working on a failed deterministic check; Codex’s corresponding hooks should be treated as context injection and validation signals, not assumed equivalent.

I would implement hooks in this order:

1. `SubagentStart` JIT context injection  
   Detect the workspace stack and role; inject only the relevant tool preference, language hazard reference, and delegation-packet reminder.

2. `PreToolUse` deterministic guardrails  
   Protect generated output, prevent unsafe direct schema mutation, and reject disallowed commands only where the repository policy is unambiguous.

3. `PostToolUse` targeted validation  
   Validate changed JSON artifacts and generated marketplace freshness only when relevant files changed—not after every edit.

4. Role-aware completion checks  
   Claude can enforce more at subagent completion; Codex should return structured evidence to the primary agent, which owns the final judgment.

We should not make hooks run broad test suites, perform network work, or make subjective quality decisions. Hooks are best for fast, deterministic boundaries; skills and role cards remain responsible for reasoning and workflow.
The hooks don't need to be shared if we can build better experience but if we can maintain one that would be ideal

Exactly. Optimize for the harness first; share only where it improves correctness and maintenance.

The right boundary is:

```text
Shared: policy, rule data, fixtures, expected outcomes
Native: hook registration, event handling, context wording, control decisions
```

Not this:

```text
One shared shell script pretending Claude and Codex have identical hook semantics
```

A good layout would be:

```text
shared/hook-policies/
  jit-context@1.json
  protected-paths@1.json
  artifact-validation@1.json

harnesses/claude/hooks/
  hooks.json
  subagent-context.<native>
  pre-tool-policy.<native>
  post-edit-validation.<native>

harnesses/codex/hooks/
  hooks.json
  subagent-context.<native>
  pre-tool-policy.<native>
  post-edit-validation.<native>

tests/fixtures/hooks/
  rust-workspace.json
  typescript-workspace.json
  protected-paths.json
```

Each harness adapter reads the same declarative policy and produces its native hook output. That gives us one source of truth for:

- Which workspace signals select a language/reference pack.
- Which paths are generated or protected.
- Which changed files require schema or marketplace validation.
- The maximum context injected for each role/event.

But the adapters remain independent where it matters:

| Concern | Share? | Why |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Language detection rules | Yes | Same observable workspace facts |
| Protected-path rules | Yes | Same safety policy |
| Validation selection | Yes | Same artifact semantics |
| Hook event wiring | No | Different event names and payloads |
| Context phrasing | No | Optimize for each model/harness |
| Block/retry behavior | No | Claude and Codex control semantics differ |
| Subagent completion workflow | No | Claude has stronger completion-hook control |
| Model/effort selection | No | Codex custom-agent capability |

I would not build a shared hook runtime yet. Start with two excellent native implementations backed by identical policy fixtures. If both adapters later contain the same pure logic—such as language detection—extract only that pure function/library.

That avoids the worst failure mode: a “shared” implementation that limits Claude to Codex’s weaker event semantics, or makes Codex carry Claude-specific complexity.
What are you thinking would be beneficial in hooks and would not cause more turn and confusion for the agents?

We should be very conservative. Most hooks would add noise, create retry loops, or duplicate instructions the skill already provides.

The rule should be: a hook earns its place only if it is deterministic, silent on success, fast, read-only or narrowly blocking, and gives one actionable failure message. No model calls, network work, broad tests, automatic formatting, or subjective review.

I would build only this now:

| Hook | Benefit | Agent impact |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Authoring source-of-truth guard | Blocks direct edits to `dist/codex`; directs the agent to edit native source then regenerate | No extra turn unless an agent makes the wrong edit |
| Immutable schema guard | Blocks edits to an already tracked `shared/schemas/*@N.json`; directs the agent to add `@N+1` | No extra turn unless an agent violates a hard rule |

Both should activate only when the workspace is recognizably this marketplace repository. They should be implemented natively for Claude and Codex, backed by the same small policy fixture and tests.

I would defer or reject these for now:

- Generic `SessionStart` context injection: AGENTS.md and skills already provide the durable context.
- Global `SubagentStart` reminders: repeats role-card instructions and consumes context.
- Post-edit formatting: creates surprising diffs.
- Post-edit test execution: slows inner loops and produces noisy failures while edits are incomplete.
- Stop hooks that force continuation: prone to loops and fights legitimate user-directed stopping.
- Automatic delegation: risks ceremony, cost, and conflicting writes.
- Any hook that depends on Wisp or Monokl: defer until their MCP contracts exist.

One possible later pilot is a narrowly scoped `SubagentStart` hook for Ranger’s language-specific scanners only: detect Rust or TypeScript and inject the one relevant hazard-reference path. It adds no separate model turn, but it does add context, so we should compare it against the existing `<load_first>` behavior before keeping it.

So the immediate hook scope is intentionally boring: protect the generated bundle and schema immutability. That gives real value without making agents feel like they are being second-guessed.
This is hooks just to this repo but as a set of hooks that ships with the plugins for both claude and codex, do we need anything right now?

No. We should not ship hooks with the plugins right now.

For an installed plugin operating in an arbitrary user workspace, we do not yet have a deterministic, cross-project behavior that belongs below the skill layer. Current skills already own routing, artifact contracts, delegation, evidence, and fallbacks.

Shipping hooks now would add trust/install friction and implicit behavior without a concrete payoff.

Keep hooks out of the distributable Claude and Codex plugins until one of these becomes real:

- Wisp exposes a stable artifact operation that must be enforced or refreshed at a lifecycle boundary.
- Monokl exposes a stable post-edit or pre-action check with a clear, low-noise failure mode.
- A plugin has a genuinely universal, deterministic safety requirement across target repositories.
- Evaluation shows a specific skill repeatedly misses a lifecycle action that a hook can safely enforce.

The existing `shared/hooks/` scripts should remain authoring/reference material for now—not shipped runtime behavior.
Ok, hooks just for this repo sounds good

I’ll add two repository-local, failure-only guards: generated Codex output is never edited by hand, and tracked schema versions are immutable. They will activate through this repo’s Claude and Codex configuration—not the distributed plugins—and do nothing in other workspaces.

content.text:
## Verdict

The packaging is strong and the Codex marketplace is genuinely installable. I independently verified all 27 tests, strict-validated all ten Claude plugins, and installed the generated Codex marketplace plus `scribe` through an isolated Codex home.

I would not yet call the cross-harness workflow behaviorally release-ready.

| Priority | Finding |
| :--- | :--- |
| P0 | The stated persistence invariant is violated across both harnesses. |
| P0 | `research-report@1` cannot supply the ID that `spec@1.linked_research` claims to reference. |
| P1 | Codex packaged-resource paths are ambiguous at runtime. |
| P1 | Codex role cards are guidance, not executable model/effort profiles. |
| P1 | No real behavioral evaluation results exist. |
| P2 | CI does not run Claude’s official plugin validator. |

### P0 — persistence is not one contract

The constitution requires a passing spec or plan to be written and committed immediately. Claude `scribe:gate-spec` and `navigator:plan` do that, but Codex requires an additional user authorization first. Codex `muse:component` writes a spec after passing but does not require authorization or require a commit. Claude Muse also omits the required commit orchestration.

This is broader than the architecture-model discrepancy Claude found: the durable lifecycle differs at several critical stages.

Relevant files: [constitution](</Users/gabe/Projects/agent-plugins/shared/constitution.md>), [Codex gate](</Users/gabe/Projects/agent-plugins/harnesses/codex/plugins/scribe/skills/gate-spec/SKILL.md>), [Codex planner](</Users/gabe/Projects/agent-plugins/harnesses/codex/plugins/navigator/skills/plan/SKILL.md>), [Codex Muse](</Users/gabe/Projects/agent-plugins/harnesses/codex/plugins/muse/skills/component/SKILL.md>).

Decide this deliberately: either persistence/commit needs fresh authorization in every harness, or it is an approved lifecycle action after a passing gate. Then make the constitution, both harnesses, and tests agree.

### P0 — the research handoff is not referentially valid

`spec@1.linked_research` says it contains the ID of a research report, but `research-report@1` has no `id` field. The compatibility fixture uses `RESEARCH-CROSS-HARNESS-001`, which cannot exist in the referenced document.

This affects Claude and Codex equally and means the core requirement → research → spec chain is not actually resolvable by contract.

Relevant files: [research schema](</Users/gabe/Projects/agent-plugins/shared/schemas/research-report@1.json>), [spec schema](</Users/gabe/Projects/agent-plugins/shared/schemas/spec@1.json>), [fixture](</Users/gabe/Projects/agent-plugins/tests/fixtures/cross-harness/lifecycle.json>).

Because schemas are immutable, fix it with a versioned contract: either add an `id` in `research-report@2`, or replace the reference with a defined durable locator such as a path plus content hash. Add referential-integrity tests, not just JSON-shape tests.

### P1 — Codex resources are present, but not deterministically addressed

Codex bundles schemas and role cards at the plugin root, while skills live at `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. Skills reference `shared/...` and `agent-roles/...` without declaring that those paths are relative to the installed plugin root or to the skill file.

The current tests prove the files were copied, not that an installed skill can resolve them from a target workspace. Make package-relative references explicit—for example, `../../shared/...` from a skill—or move skill-local dependencies under each skill’s `references/` directory. Add a test that resolves every declared runtime reference from the owning `SKILL.md`.

Claude has a related local-development limitation: its marketplace installation can dereference same-marketplace symlinks, but local `--plugin-dir` and local-path installs skip symlinks that point outside the plugin directory. That is documented Claude behavior. [Claude plugin caching reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins-reference)

### P1 — role cards do not yet deliver model routing

The role cards are good cognitive-boundary guidance, but there are no Codex TOML agent profiles in the repository. Therefore `gpt-5.6-*` tiers are recommendations, not host-enforced routing, and agent teams get generic subagents unless the user separately configured them.

This is an intentional marketplace limitation, not a packaging defect: current Codex supports custom project/user TOML subagents, but plugins do not automatically install them. The right next layer is an opt-in companion profile set plus an installer/activation guide—not embedding TOML as an implicit plugin contract. [Codex subagents](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/subagents)

### P1 — behavioral evaluation is specified, not performed

The evaluation protocol is thoughtful, but there are no recorded runs under `docs/evaluations/`. Structural parity cannot demonstrate that the Codex single-agent and team paths produce durable, evidence-grounded artifacts.

Run the three defined core cases before public claims about cross-harness quality:

1. Claude workflow
2. Codex single-agent workflow
3. Codex team workflow with actual role/model settings recorded

### P2 — strengthen Claude CI

All ten Claude plugins pass `claude plugin validate --strict` locally. CI does not run that validator, so a future Claude-only incompatibility can pass repository checks. Add a reproducible Claude validation job or a pinned validator action.

## What is solid

- Codex CLI marketplace commands, `plugin@marketplace` selection, generated marketplace structure, and local installation are correct.
- The generator’s atomicity, symlink containment, source/native skill parity, version and author matching are well tested.
- The shared commit guard uses a valid Codex PreToolUse payload and valid legacy block response. [Codex hooks](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/hooks)
- The choice not to mechanically generate Codex prompt bodies from Claude prompts is correct.

I made no changes.
What would the changes look like? Show me

Yes. I’d make this a targeted hardening pass, not a redesign.

```text
                     Shared lifecycle contract
                               │
        ┌──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
        │                      │                      │
 Claude source            Codex native source      Contract tests
 skills + agents          skills + role cards      links + policy + paths
        │                      │
        │                      ├── generated marketplace
        │                      │
        │                      └── optional TOML profiles
        │                              │
        └──────── durable JSON ────────┴──► target project's .codex/agents/
```

## 1. Make persistence policy explicit and identical

Instead of the constitution requiring every passing artifact to commit automatically, define authorization as part of the lifecycle contract.

```md
## Durable Artifact Authorization

WHEN a user explicitly authorizes persistence of a passing artifact, the producing skill SHALL write the artifact to its durable path, set its path field, and create the prescribed commit.

IF that authorization is absent, the producing skill SHALL return the passing artifact and proposed persistence action without writing or committing it.

WHEN an artifact is persisted, both harnesses SHALL use the same path, schema version, and commit requirement.
```

Then the same semantic flow appears in both harnesses:

```text
draft → audit → gate pass
                 │
                 ├── no authority → return artifact + exact proposed write
                 │
                 └── authority → write → commit → hand off durable artifact
```

This changes Claude `scribe`, `navigator`, and `muse` to match the safer Codex behavior, and changes Codex Muse to require authorization and commit after persistence.

## 2. Repair the research identity contract with v2 schemas

The new chain should carry an actual durable reference, not an invented string ID.

```json
{
  "id": "RESEARCH-PLUGIN-MARKETPLACE-001",
  "report_file_path": "docs/research/RESEARCH-PLUGIN-MARKETPLACE-001.json",
  "question": "…",
  "findings": [],
  "recommendation": "…",
  "confidence": "high",
  "open_questions": []
}
```

Then `spec@2` references it structurally:

```json
{
  "research_inputs": [
    {
      "schema": "research-report@2",
      "id": "RESEARCH-PLUGIN-MARKETPLACE-001",

```

research-report@2 ── durable ID + durable path

spec@1            ── retained
spec@2            ── structured research references

plan@1            ── retained
plan@2            ── explicitly consumes spec@2
```

Both harnesses can support v1 and v2 during migration. New workflows produce v2; old artifacts remain readable.

## 3. Make Codex package-resource paths deterministic

Current Codex skills say:

```md

Read `agent-roles/README.md`.
```

All paths below are relative to this `SKILL.md` file.

- Schema: `../../shared/schemas/spec@2.json`
- Role packet guide: `../../agent-roles/README.md`
- Role card: `../../agent-roles/reviewer.md`
```

The generated layout stays efficient:

```text
plugins/scribe/
├── skills/gate-spec/SKILL.md
├── agent-roles/reviewer.md
└── shared/schemas/spec@2.json
```

But now every reference has a mechanically testable meaning. A new test resolves each declared packaged path from the owning `SKILL.md` and fails if it does not exist.

```text
harnesses/codex/
├── agent-roles/
│   ├── recon.md
│   ├── adversary.md
│   └── judge.md
├── agent-profiles/
│   ├── orin-recon.toml
│   ├── orin-adversary.toml
│   └── orin-judge.toml
└── install-agent-profiles.py
```

Example:

```toml
name = "orin-adversary"
description = "Independently falsifies a bounded implementation or artifact claim."
model = "gpt-5.6-terra"
model_reasoning_effort = "high"
sandbox_mode = "read-only"

developer_instructions = """
Seek evidence-backed counterexamples only.
Do not edit files, issue a final verdict, or treat suspicion as a defect.

"""

Installation remains explicit and safe:

```bash
python3 tools/install-codex-agent-profiles.py --project .
```

That writes profiles to:

```text
target-project/.codex/agents/
```

Codex skills then use this rule:

```text
Use an installed `orin-<role>` profile when available.
Otherwise delegate with the packaged role card and packet.
Otherwise complete the bounded pass in the primary agent.
```

This gives you real Codex-native routing without pretending TOML is automatically installed by a marketplace plugin. [Codex custom subagents](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/subagents)

content.text:
Yes: don’t create eight TOML files that duplicate eight role cards.

Separate the two concerns:

```text
Role card = what cognitive job to do
Runtime profile = model, effort, sandbox, concurrency characteristics
Skill = when to use each combination and what packet to send
```

```text
              ┌──────────────────────────┐
              │ Codex skill              │
              │ “need independent audit” │
              └────────────┬─────────────┘
                           │
               selects role + runtime profile
                           │
          ┌────────────────┴────────────────┐
          │                                 │
┌─────────▼──────────┐            ┌─────────▼────────────┐
│ `adversary.md`     │            │ `orin-critic.toml`   │
│ evidence standard  │            │ Terra / high          │
│ no edits           │            │ read-only sandbox     │
│ return format      │            │ bounded instructions  │
└────────────────────┘            └──────────────────────┘
```

I would use five Codex runtime profiles, not eight role-specific profiles:

| Runtime profile | Model / effort | Sandbox | Roles using it |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `orin-scout` | Luna / low | read-only | recon |
| `orin-analyst` | Terra / medium | read-only | tracer, research |
| `orin-critic` | Terra / high | read-only | adversary, reviewer |
| `orin-builder` | Terra / high | workspace-write | implementer |
| `orin-judge` | Sol / high | read-only | judge |

`author` generally does not need its own profile: the primary agent should author the durable result, while a delegated author returns a bounded draft under `orin-analyst` or `orin-critic`, depending on the task.

That avoids this bad shape:

```text
adversary.md  ── duplicated into ── adversary.toml
reviewer.md   ── duplicated into ── reviewer.toml
judge.md      ── duplicated into ── judge.toml
```

The role card remains the semantic source of truth. The TOML profile is only the execution envelope.

```toml
name = "orin-critic"
description = "Read-only high-effort independent review and counterexample search."
model = "gpt-5.6-terra"
model_reasoning_effort = "high"
sandbox_mode = "read-only"

developer_instructions = """
Work only within the parent’s bounded packet.
Do not edit files, make external changes, or issue the final decision.
Read primary evidence directly and return evidence-backed findings or an explicit no-finding result.
"""
```

Then the skill supplies the rich role instruction and packet:

```text
Delegate with:
- runtime profile: `orin-critic`
- role card: `agent-roles/adversary.md`
- objective: falsify criterion AC-004
- inputs: spec path, changed files, baseline command
- ownership: read-only
- evidence: exact locations and a reproducible failing scenario
```

This is better than treating TOML as the role itself.

## What Codex is missing

Codex does support custom TOML subagents in `.codex/agents/` or `~/.codex/agents/`, including model, reasoning effort, sandbox, MCP, and skill configuration. But those are project/user configuration layers—not a first-class plugin component with namespaced installation and discovery. [Official Codex subagent documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/subagents)

Claude plugins have a cleaner packaging story here: a plugin’s `agents/` directory is discovered as plugin-scoped agents. Codex currently has:

```text
Plugin package      → skills, MCP, hooks, assets
Project config      → .codex/agents/*.toml
User config         → ~/.codex/agents/*.toml
```

So yes: there is a real platform gap around portable, plugin-owned agent profiles.

## How others are handling it

Most Codex agent libraries simply ship one TOML per role and tell users to copy selected files into `.codex/agents/` or `~/.codex/agents/`. Examples include [VoltAgent’s collection](https://github.com/VoltAgent/awesome-codex-subagents) and [CodeDraig’s catalog](https://github.com/CodeDraig/codex-subagents). That works, but it tends to duplicate prompt intent and produce large, overlapping agent catalogs.

I’d do better:

```text
Plugin marketplace
├── packaged role cards
├── skills that select role + profile
└── profile templates, not auto-installed

Target project
└── .codex/agents/
    ├── orin-scout.toml
    ├── orin-analyst.toml
    ├── orin-critic.toml
    ├── orin-builder.toml
    └── orin-judge.toml
```

Use an explicit installer or copier for the target project. It should never silently write configuration. Once installed, skills can prefer the named profile; without it, they pass the same role card to a generic subagent or run sequentially.

That gives us portability, model routing, graceful fallback, and no duplicated eight-agent prompt zoo.
